title: Optimal exercise type and dose to improve sleep quality in older adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis

sections.abstract:
Sleep quality decreased can result in a major health issue in older people with age. While not all sleep changes are pathological in older people’s life, severe disturbances may lead to depression, cognitive impairments, deterioration of quality of life, significant stresses for careers and increased healthcare costs. Despite the known benefits of exercise for improving sleep quality, it is necessary to identify the optimal exercise type and dose.

This systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) combined to examine evaluated the existing evidence on the effectiveness of different exercises, and to examine the dose and response relationship between overall and specific types with improving sleep quality in older people.

PubMed, Cochrane Central, Web of Science, and Embase were systematically searched for this review, including studies up to April 2025. Only randomized controlled trials were included. Studies involved at least one type of exercise intervention and reported changes in sleep quality assessments. To address the limitations of relying solely on statistical significance, we also calculated the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) to determine the smallest meaningful improvement in sleep quality among older people, both overall and across different exercise doses. Data analysis and visualization were conducted using the “meta”, “netmeta”, “MBNMA”, and “ggplot2” packages in the R environment.

A total of 62 RCTs involving 5005 older adults were included. Overall, exercise significantly improved sleep quality, with clinically meaningful improvements achieved from as early as 5 weeks of intervention. The optimal exercise type was combined aerobic and resistance training, followed by aerobic exercise, resistance training, walking, and yoga. The estimated optimal exercise dose was around 660 to 990 METs*min/week, with longer durations at 15 weeks producing the greatest benefits. Improvements were more pronounced among participants with poorer baseline sleep quality.

If older people receive the most appropriate exercise intervention, they can obtain clinically meaningful benefits of improving sleep in the elderly within the WHO guidelines for exercise doses. The results support the WHO recommendation that combine aerobic exercise and resistance training should be an important part of interventions for the older people.

PROSPERO registration number: CRD42024566751.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12877-025-06607-z.
sections.introduction:
Sleep disturbances are common among older adults, affecting more than half of this population and reaching rates as high as 70% [ 1 ]. Poor sleep not only diminishes quality of life, but also contributes to the development and worsening of physical and mental health conditions, ultimately increasing the risk of mortality [ 2 – 4 ]. In addition, sleep loss is linked to significant memory impairments and may indirectly raise the risk of Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia [ 5 ]. As the global older adult population continues to grow [ 6 ], enhancing sleep quality in this demographic should be a key public health priority to promote healthier aging.

Notably, due to the economy and “pharmacology” of exercise, a number of studies have focused more on the role of exercise in older adults and maximizing the potential of exercise in terms of its impact on older adults [ 7 , 8 ]. For example, Santos et al. were the first to propose the hypothesis that exercise regulates the plasma concentration of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which could subsequently influence the physiological mechanisms underlying sleep [ 9 ]. Similarly, the study results of Tan et.al. show that exercise-induced skeletal muscle recruitment increases blood levels of a signaling molecule (brain-derived neurotrophic factor, BDNF) that can increase the depth of sleep [ 10 ]. Additionally, a prospective study result by Tsunoda et.al. illustrated low to moderate exercise can effectively maintain adequate sleep for the elderly [ 11 ].

Previous meta-analyses consistently suggest that exercise improves sleep in older adults [ 12 ]. However, their conclusions about the most effective exercise type are inconsistent. For example, some network meta-analyses identified combined endurance training with walking [ 13 ], mind–body exercise [ 14 ], or Qigong [ 15 ] as optimal, while others favored aerobic training [ 16 ]. Although previous studies have shown promising results, these findings yield conflicting conclusions regarding the best form of exercise. In addition, disagreements persist due to variations in exercise type, participant characteristics, and study methodologies. These controversies highlight the need for further comprehensive research to clarify which exercise intervention is most effective in improving sleep quality in older adults.

At the same time, as with this previous evidence, we think that the effectiveness of different types of exercise may depend on varying dosages for improving sleep quality. According to the WHO guidelines, older adults should engage in at least 150 min of moderate-intensity or 75 min of vigorous-intensity physical activity per week [ 17 ]. Therefore, It is important to consider the impact of different doses on sleep quality to achieve optimal, and personalized exercise prescriptions [ 18 ]. Additionally, some previous studies have proved the nonlinear relationship between different exercise doses and different outcomes on older adults [ 19 – 21 ], and we will use the previous method on using our study to analyze exercise dose and the response improvement of sleep quality.

To provide a more comprehensive systematic analysis, we conducted a more comprehensive analysis conducted paired meta-analysis, network meta-analysis, and Bayesian dose–response network meta-analysis to produce more detailed and reliable evidence for the clinical promotion of exercise aimed at improving sleep quality in the elderly. Additionally, we considered the impact of Type I error, which may lead to fail to detect some actual intervention effects, thereby overestimating the effectiveness of the intervention [ 22 ]. To avoid potential misjudgment, we focused on identifying the true effective response population, defined as participants whose improvements exceeded the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) threshold [ 23 ]. Accordingly, we analyzed exercise types and doses in relation to this population to capture the true treatment effect. This approach distinguishes responders from non-responders and enhances the validity of our conclusions. Furthermore, by calculating the MCID, we were able to determine the exercise doses associated with clinically meaningful improvements, thereby strengthening the clinical relevance of our findings [ 24 ]. Our study aims to contribute significantly to evidence-based exercise guidelines for improving sleep quality in the elderly and to assist medical professionals in decision-making.

Finally, there were 62 RCT studies included in the systematic review and meta-analysis (see Fig. 1 ), and we provided an included list in Supplementary File 6. A total of 5005 older adults with a mean age of 68 years were included in our study. The detailed characteristics of the included studies’ related information are provided in Table 1 . The meta-analysis results indicated that the effect of overall exercise on sleep quality in older adults was significant (SMD: −0.68, 95% CI: −0.85 to −0.51, p = 0.01) compared with the comparator/control group. The dose–response relationship curve illustrated the nonlinear relationship between the overall exercise dose and the response to the improvement of sleep quality in Fig. 3 B. The effective dose range was estimated to be from 320 to 1400 METs*min/week, with the optimal overall exercise dose estimated at 990 METs*min/week (SMD: −0.858, 95%Crl: −1.192 to −0.497). Worthily, the WHO official guide dose recommended for physical exercise (600 to 1200 METs*min/week) is also within the effective dose range.

Figure 4 A illustrated the effective treatment ranking of different exercises, AE + RT showed the highest efficacy with an SMD of −1.71 (95% CI: −2.28 to −1.14, P-score: 1.00). This was followed by AE with an SMD of −0.96 (95% CI: −1.27 to −0.65, P-score: 0.77) and RT with an SMD of −0.85 (95% CI: −1.30 to −0.39, P-score: 0.65). Yoga, Qigong, VR, Walking, and Taichi also showed significant improvements with SMD of −0.77, −0.74, −0.67, −0.66, and −0.45, respectively, and corresponding P-scores. Figure 4 B illustrated the nonlinear relationship between different exercise doses and the improvement of sleep quality, we found the optimal dose of AE + RT 1000 METs*min/week (SMD: −1.942, 95% CrI: −3.105 to −0.778) and the effective dose of it was estimated from 540 to 1000 METs*min/week. Additionally, we found RT, AE, Walking, and Yoga showed a slightly inverted U shape and they existed the optimal peak dose. We found the RT effective range dose was estimated from 250 to 880 METs*min/week, and the optimal RT dose was estimated at 560 METs*min/week (SMD: −1.231, 95% CrI: −2.159 to −0.287). Behind this, the AE effective range dose was estimated from 290 to 1100 METs*min/week, and the optimal dose of AE was estimated at 810 METs*min/week (SMD: −1.1003, 95% CrI: −1.606 to −0.577). Interestingly, we found a walking maximum dose close to 2000 METs*min/week, in which the walking effective range dose was estimated from 750 to 1300 METs*min/week with the optimal Walking dose estimated at 1200 METs*min/week (SMD: −0.807, 95% CrI: −1.582 to −0.049). Finally, the Yoga effective range dose was estimated from 320 to 670 METs*min/week, and the optimal Yoga dose was estimated at 540 METs*min/week (SMD: −0.718, 95% CrI: −1.317 to −1.001). Surprisingly, we found the exercise types of Mix, Qigong, Taichi, and VR had no significant effect at any dose.

The pooled effect size equivalent to the estimated MCID for PSQI was large (SMD: −0.69, 95% CI: −0.86 to −0.52) and the minimal predicted dose of overall exercise needed to achieve this effect was 660 METs*min/week. Corresponding values were 380 METs*min/week for AE, 260 METs*min/week for RT, 830 METs*min/week for Walking, and 460 METs*min/week for Yoga. And we visualize the results of MCID in every curve plot. However, we also found mixed exercise, Qigong, Tai Chi, and virtual reality interventions did not achieve clinically meaningful improvements in sleep quality.

Additionally, through focusing on subtle stratification of exercise intensity, such as light-intensity exercise programs (< 3 METs, such as walking, doing housework) and moderate-intensity exercise (3–6 METs, such as brisk walking, cycling) (see Fig. 5 A), the results showed that although light intensity exercise still provided clinically meaningful effects, the expected effects of moderate-intensity exercise were stronger and exceeded the MCID threshold. In addition, we analyzed the relationship between the exercise period of the included studies and the improvement of sleep quality. The results showed that the optimal improvement effect appeared at 15 weeks (SMD: 1.002, 95% CrI: −1.244 to −0.759), and the MCID appeared at about 5 weeks, which is a clinically meaningful benefit within this range (see Fig. 5 B). In a meta-regression analysis, we examined the effects of covariates such as number of exercises per week, exercise frequency, duration of a single exercise session, sample size, proportion of men, proportion of women, presence of disease, and mean age. All analytical results are detailed in Table S15. The results showed that none of these covariates had a statistically significant impact on the effectiveness of exercise intervention in improving sleep quality.

However, based on the evidence from previous studies and considerations of clinical practice [ 46 , 47 ], we further explored the relationship between the efficacy of exercise intervention and baseline sleep quality scores and age in the elderly (see Fig. 6 ). The results show that exercise intervention has a more significant effect on older people with higher baseline sleep quality scores (representing poorer sleep quality), especially in the older age group. Specifically, the higher the baseline sleep quality score, the more significant the improvement effect of exercise intervention. In addition, age also affects the efficacy of exercise intervention. The analysis shows that the overall efficacy of the elderly group between 60 and 70 years old is relatively weak, while the distribution of efficacy in the more elderly is more scattered, with significant individual differences. Thirteen (21%) studies had a low risk of bias, 45 (73%) studies had a moderate risk of bias, and 4 (6%) studies had a high risk of bias (see Fig. 7 ), meanwhile, we provided a heat map of study-level risk of bias assessment result in Fig. S12 to S13. The overall quality of the evidence was moderate according to the GRADE system. Fig. 7 RoB 2 heat map

RoB 2 heat map

When examining CINeMA, certain domains related to within-study bias, reporting bias, and imprecision raised “low risk” in most comparisons, with percentages of 84.6%, 94.32%, and 61.35%, separately. On the other hand, the domains of indirectness, heterogeneity, and incoherence did not raise concerns in most comparisons, with percentages of 80.6%, 50.34%, and 90.2%, separately. We provided detailed reports’ results in Fig. S14-S16, and Table S16.

In the sensitivity analysis, we excluded 4 studies that were assessed as high-risk and re-performed the paired-meta-analysis which the results showed was robust to the results before exclusion (SMD: −0.67, 95% CI: −0.82, −0.53) (See Supplementary Fig. 31). And, we conducted the sensitivity analysis of network meta-analysis, which results illustrated the AE + RT still is the most effective exercise to improve sleep quality, but we also found treatment effective ranking changes for the Qigong (SMD: −0.79, 95% CI: −1.36 to −0.23, P = 0.59) higher effective than Yoga (SMD: −0.77, 95% CI: −1.10 to −0.44, P = 0.58), and the Walking (SMD: −0.76, 95% CI: −1.13 to −0.39, P = 0.56) higher effective than VR (SMD: −0.65, 95% CI: −1.28 to −0.01, P = 0.47) after excluded high level risk articles (See Fig. S18). At the same time, we perform the sensitivity analysis of overall exercise dose and response of improvement sleep quality, which result illustrated the effective effect exercise dose was estimated 300 to 1400 METs-min/week with the optimal at 1000 METs-min/week (SMD: −0.701, 95% CrI: −1.209 to −0.508) (See Fig. S21).

Additionally, to deeply prove our research results’ robustness, we only included healthy old adults to analyze all results, and the results illustrated the close effective results exercise group compared to the control group in healthy older adults (SMD: −0.70, 95% CI: −0.85 to −0.56, I 2 = 63.8%) (See Fig. S22). At the same time, we also analyzed the ranking of exercise in improving sleep quality in healthy elderly people and the overall exercise dose–response relationship. All analysis results have not been found to be significantly different from the original data (See Fig. S23 & S24).
sections.discussion:
Our study included 62 studies with a total of 5,005 older adults and 9 types of exercise. Our paired meta-analysis results demonstrated that participating in exercise significantly improves sleep quality compared to the control group. Notably, this is the first study to identify an optimal overall exercise dose of 990 METs-min/week, aligning with the WHO’s recommended range of 600–1,200 MET-min/week [ 48 ]. Importantly, the analysis result of effective response rates showed that the incidence of effective events in sleep quality improvement was significantly higher in the exercise group than in the control group. The optimal incidence rate of effective events for the overall exercise dose was estimated at 910 METs*min/week, indirectly confirming the effectiveness of the estimated dose of approximately 990 METs*min/week. Additionally, our network meta-analysis identified AE + RT as the most effective exercise type. Furthermore, in the dose–response network meta-analysis, AE + RT emerged as the optimal exercise at 1,000 METs-min/week.

This study breaks through the established evidence of the benefits of exercise and provides a more precise understanding of how much exercise can bring about optimal improvements, thereby advancing the field of exercise and sleep research in the elderly [ 49 ]. However, it is different from previous research, we are the first to establish a nonlinear relationship between overall exercise and sleep quality improvements in this population. By identifying a nonlinear relationship between exercise level and sleep quality, our findings emphasize that excessive exercise does not necessarily provide additional benefits, and that moderate exercise is most effective. Clinicians can now consider tailoring exercise prescriptions, rather than prescribing them in general, to maximize sleep quality in older adults. For example, incorporating moderate-intensity exercise, or a combination of aerobic and resistance exercise, into a weekly routine may be an effective and sustainable way to improve sleep quality without placing an excessive burden on patients. These insights can help refine exercise guidelines and support the integration of personalized exercise prescriptions into geriatric care. We also identified an effective dose range that aligns with WHO-recommended exercise intensities, and we determined the optimal exercise dose to enhance sleep quality in older adults.

Our network meta-analysis results are consistent with those of Hasan et al. [ 13 ], indicating that the combination of AE + RT is the most effective approach to improving sleep quality among the older people. However, Hasan et al.’s study lacks strong clinical significance regarding exercise intensity. Furthermore, the small sample size limits the ability to determine the long-term therapeutic effects of various exercise programs, presenting a key limitation of their study. Importantly, our research is the first to use task metabolic equivalents as the standard for assessing exercise intensity.

Our study presents several valuable strengths. We conducted a meta-regression analysis to explore the impact of effect moderators, including exercise program duration (weeks), frequency (times/week), session length (minutes), sample size, percentage of male and female participants, baseline PSQI score, presence of disease, and average age, whether there is any disease and average age, on the results. The results showed no significant differences in effectiveness across these covariates, indicating that exercise reliably improves sleep quality in older adults regardless of these factors.

To enhance the clinical applicability of our research, we incorporated insights from previous studies and clinical significance to further analyze the relationship between the effect of exercise intervention in the elderly and baseline sleep quality scores and age [ 46 , 47 ]. The results found that the higher the baseline sleep quality score, the better. High, the more significant the effect of exercise intervention is, indicating that the elderly with more serious sleep problems have greater room for improvement, and the impact of exercise intervention is more obvious. This is also consistent with previous research on the benefits of exercise on sleep quality in people with sleep disorders [ 50 ]. We also found that exercise intervention was more effective for elderly people with high baseline sleep scores, especially the elderly (> 70 years old), which is comparable to the results of a previous physiological mechanism study, which showed that regular exercise can effectively improve the sleep of elderly rats’ architecture and core temperature physiology disrupted by age [ 51 ]. Therefore, our results are consistent with past studies and suggest that it should be promoted first in the high baseline score group, and more personalized intervention measures should be designed for the elderly group to improve efficacy. This also greatly confirms the universality of our research results.

Our network meta-analysis results also confirmed that AE, RT, Yoga, Qigong, VR, Walking, and Taichi can effectively improve the sleep quality of older people. However, in the dose–response analysis, Qigong, Taichi, VR, and Mixed exercises did not show significant improvements at any specific dose. We have explored potential underlying mechanisms to explain these differences. AE and Walking, as aerobic exercises, have a unique and powerful sleep-promoting effect, including exercise promotes body temperature regulation [ 52 ], exercise improves the compensatory mechanism of physical recovery [ 53 ], the energy conservation hypothesis [ 54 ], These may be the key to improving sleep quality in the presence of effective doses of AE and walking.

Additionally, the mechanisms by which resistance exercise alters sleep, and whether this benefit is mediated in part by psychological, physiological, or neurobiological changes, remain largely unclear. However, we found that resistance training may improve sleep by improving symptoms of depression or anxiety, altering energy expenditure, increasing body temperature, or relieving musculoskeletal pain [ 55 ], and the adaptability of the intensity of RT to the physical differences of different older adults and the release of hormones related to recovery and repair [ 56 ], these may be the key to the dose–response relationship of RT in changing the sleep quality of older adults.

Surprisingly, our study also found the effectiveness of yoga, Qigong, and Taichi, which is consistent with the study of He et al. [ 15 ]. However, compared with Qigong and Taichi, our results only found a dose–response relationship for yoga and an effective dose range for improving sleep quality and did not find the effectiveness of Qigong and Taichi at any dose. There are some reasons that the broad and varied components of yoga interventions (asanas, pranayama, meditation, philosophical teachings) [ 57 ], and the strongest empirical evidence suggests that yoga’s ability to regulate hormones is a factor in providing health benefits, with regular practice leading to lower cortisol levels and higher serotonin and melatonin levels [ 58 ], these show the advantages of yoga over Qigong and Taichi, this indirectly becomes a key factor in the dose–response effect of yoga.

In addition, VR is a potential intervention. We found that virtual reality intervention can effectively improve the sleep quality of the elderly, but VR did not show significant effects at any dose. This may suggest that the effects of VR are independent of the intensity or frequency of the intervention, perhaps because it relies on specific usage or context rather than a simple dose factor. Future research needs to further explore standardizing session length, comparing different content types (e.g., relaxation versus interactive experiences), assessing comfort and usability in older adults, and exploring individual preference and acceptance. Such refinements may clarify how VR can be optimized as a sleep-enhancing intervention [ 59 ].

Finally, we used the bias risk assessment tool to conduct a more in-depth assessment of the included studies in order to promote the research results in clinical practice. It is valuable that we adopted the reviewers’ opinions and conducted a sensitivity analysis of the main data results after excluding some studies with a high risk of bias and some studies with clinical disease reports. The results consistently showed that our research results have good robustness.

Table 2 offers valuable exercise recommendations for improving sleep quality in older adults from this review main results. The table lists different types of exercise, their energy expenditure in MET*min/week, intensity levels, and corresponding relative intensity (expressed as a percentage of HRmax or 1 RM). In addition, it provides recommended cumulative weekly exercise volumes, along with guidance on frequency and training duration, emphasizing both the optimal and minimally effective exercise doses needed to enhance sleep quality. Additionally, our study is valuable not only for identifying the effective dose range and peak improvement for different exercises but also for calculating the MCID. MCID serves as a threshold indicating when an individual or group begins to experience meaningful improvements. This calculation is unprecedented in previous studies, allowing us to assess the clinical effectiveness of the intervention based on whether the improvement in sleep quality exceeds the MCID, rather than relying solely on statistical significance [ 60 ]. Our findings indicate that the overall exercise dose has a minimum clinically important difference of 660 METs*min/week, which also falls within the range of exercise doses officially recommended by the WHO. Additionally, the minimum clinically important differences for specific exercises were found to be 380 METs*min/week for AE, 260 METs*min/week for RT, 830 METs*min/week for walking, and 460 METs*min/week for yoga. These results apply to clinical practice, emphasizing the subjective experiences of older adults and aligning research outcomes with the actual needs of older adults. It is worth noting that finely stratifying exercise intensity found that although light-intensity exercise can provide clinically significant improvements, the effect of moderate-intensity exercise is more significant, and the improvement exceeds the lowest MCID. It also indirectly emphasizes the effectiveness of increasing exercise intensity, which is comparable to previous research, which believes that Moderate-intensity exercise has an actual effect on the sleep quality of the elderly [ 61 ]. Worthily, research results revealed exercise intervention can significantly improve sleep quality in poorer sleep quality score older people, especially in older age people.

In addition, there has been a lack of systematic research on the long-term effects of exercise and the appropriate intervention period. A long-term exercise intervention time may cause the effect to plateau or decline slightly, possibly related to the participants’ reduced compliance, enhanced physical adaptability, and inter-individual differences related [ 62 ]. Therefore, we specifically analyzed the nonlinear relationship between the duration of exercise intervention and sleep quality improvement to provide a more comprehensive basis for clinical practice. Our research results found that MCID can be reached in about 5 weeks of exercise, but the best effect occurs in the 15th week. The accumulation of exercise intervention effects takes a certain amount of time, rather than simply increasing linearly as the intervention time is extended. The effect of an intervention that exceeds 15 weeks may tend to plateau or even decline slightly, which suggests that an intervention that is too long may be affected by reduced participant compliance, physiological adaptation, or accumulation of fatigue [ 63 ]. Therefore, identifying 15 weeks as an optimal duration highlights the importance of incorporating adherence strategies, such as progressive goal setting, social support, and variety in exercise modalities to help older adults maintain engagement and sustain benefits beyond this period. This finding of our study provides important inspiration for clinical practice, setting the intervention period to at least 5 weeks to achieve basic clinical significance, and optimizing the target intervention time to 15 weeks for the best effect. In addition, future studies can further explore how to optimize the intervention time according to individual differences (such as age, and type of sleep disorder) to achieve more personalized intervention effects.

Although our study found valuable research strengths, there are also some limitations in our study. Firstly, our study used MET values ​​to standardize exercise intensity, but MET estimates for specific activities vary according to body composition, gender, and age, and are not personalized based on physical condition [ 18 ]. When defining exercise intensity, we only attempted to effectively estimate the clinically effective threshold. Second, although our study determined that AE + RT was the most effective method and had the optimal dose, the timing of the intervention component during the intervention period was an unresolved issue in our study, and our findings only provide exercise prescription recommendations to the extent possible based on existing evidence. Third, our study relied on common scales to assess sleep quality, specifically the PSQI, ISI, and PDSS. Although these tools are widely used, their subscales may provide more specific insights into sleep quality outcomes related to exercise interventions. Therefore, our results may not fully reflect the subtle effects of different exercise methods on sleep quality. Future studies should explore these subtle effects more comprehensively. Fourth, even though we demonstrated the robustness of our findings through sensitivity analysis, the heterogeneity between studies is also an issue that cannot be ignored. Therefore, our results should be interpreted and applied clinically with caution. Fifth, when we performed meta-regression on the baseline sleep quality score, we only explored the relationship between the overall exercise intervention effect and the baseline sleep quality score and age of the elderly. In the future, we expect more studies to support the relationship between different exercise intervention effects and baseline sleep quality scores and age to confirm the feasibility of our research. Finally, to further validate our findings, studies involving larger sample sizes, greater homogeneity, and using standardized measurement methods are recommended. Additionally, this review was limited to studies published in English, which may have introduced language bias and resulted in the exclusion of relevant evidence published in other languages. Another limitation of this review is that cultural and environmental differences, which may substantially influence the feasibility and acceptability of exercise interventions among older adults, were not fully addressed. Factors such as cultural norms, social support, access to facilities, and climate conditions could affect participation and adherence, potentially limiting the generalizability of our findings across diverse settings.

sections.conclusion: Our analysis showed that exercise significantly improves sleep quality in the older people. The dose–response analysis identified an optimal dose of 990 METs*min/week, aligning with WHO recommendations. The optimal exercise type and dose was also identified as AE + RT at approximately 1000 METs-min/week, corresponding to about 3 sessions of 42 min or 5 sessions of 47 min per week. And we found the optimal exercise week at 15 weeks with MCID at 5 weeks. AE + RT was the most effective, and MCID doses for overall exercise, AE, RT, Walking, and Yoga met clinical improvement criteria. These findings highlight the need for personalized exercise prescriptions in clinical practice, supporting the integration of tailored exercise programs into elderly health management.
